summary: Ramelteon is a selective melatonin MT1/MT2 receptor agonist used to treat insomnia characterised by difficulty with sleep onset. Unlike benzodiazepine and Z-drug hypnotics it has no appreciable affinity for GABA receptors, is NOT a controlled substance, and has not shown evidence of abuse or dependence. It is rapidly absorbed, has extensive first-pass metabolism (mainly via CYP1A2), and should be taken within 30 minutes of bedtime, not with a high-fat meal. Caution is required in hepatic impairment and with the strong CYP1A2 inhibitor fluvoxamine, which is contraindicated.
indications: Treatment of insomnia characterised by difficulty with sleep onset

dosage.d: 8 mg PO once within 30 minutes of going to bed
dosage.n: Do not exceed 8 mg; do not take with or right after a high-fat meal
Use cautiously; not recommended in severe hepatic impairment

dosage.d: 8 mg PO at bedtime (no specific dose reduction required)

admin: Take within 30 minutes of going to bed and confine activities to those needed to prepare for sleep
Do not take with or immediately after a high-fat, heavy meal
Allow at least 7-8 hours in bed before planned awakening
Do not engage in activities requiring full alertness after dosing
Re-evaluate if insomnia does not improve within 7-10 days
moa: Ramelteon is a potent, selective agonist at melatonin MT1 and MT2 receptors in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, the brain's master circadian clock. Activating these receptors is believed to promote sleep onset by regulating the sleep-wake cycle. It has essentially no affinity for GABA, benzodiazepine, opioid, dopamine or serotonin receptors, which accounts for the lack of abuse potential.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to ramelteon or its components (including angioedema reactions)
Concurrent use with fluvoxamine (strong CYP1A2 inhibitor - greatly increases ramelteon exposure)
relative: Severe sleep apnea or severe COPD (not adequately studied)
History of complex sleep behaviors on hypnotics
monitor: Persistence/worsening of insomnia or emergence of new behavioral changes
Signs of complex sleep behaviors (sleep-driving, sleep-eating)

preg: Human data are limited. Animal studies showed developmental toxicity at high doses. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: Ramelteon is excreted in the milk of lactating animals; human data are lacking. Because of the potential for adverse effects in a breastfed infant, use with caution and consider the importance of the drug to the mother.
renal: No dose adjustment is required in renal impairment, including in patients on dialysis. Pharmacokinetics are not meaningfully altered by reduced renal function.
hepatic: Ramelteon undergoes extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism. Exposure is increased in hepatic impairment. Use with caution in moderate impairment and avoid in severe hepatic impairment.

major: Fluvoxamine (strong CYP1A2 inhibitor) increases ramelteon exposure roughly 190-fold - contraindicated
Strong CYP enzyme inducers such as rifampin markedly decrease ramelteon exposure and may reduce efficacy
moderate: Other CYP1A2 inhibitors (e.g., ciprofloxacin) - use with caution, increased exposure
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole) and CYP2C9 inhibitors (e.g., fluconazole) increase exposure
Other CNS depressants and hypnotics (additive sedation)
minor: Donepezil and doxepin may modestly increase ramelteon exposure
interactions.food: A high-fat meal delays time to peak and reduces effectiveness - do not take with or right after such a meal
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol; additive impairment of psychomotor and cognitive performance
interactions.diagnostics: May decrease serum cortisol and testosterone and increase prolactin in some patients; consider with unexplained endocrine symptoms (amenorrhea, galactorrhea, decreased libido)

serious: Complex sleep-related behaviors (sleep-driving, sleep-cooking/eating) with amnesia
Worsening of depression or suicidal ideation
rare: Decreased blood cortisol/testosterone, increased prolactin with endocrine symptoms (amenorrhea, galactorrhea, reduced libido, fertility problems)
emergency: Angioedema involving tongue/glottis/larynx with airway compromise

monitoring: Response of insomnia within 7-10 days; reassess if no improvement
Emergence of complex sleep behaviors or new/worsening behavioral or mood changes
Endocrine symptoms (menstrual changes, galactorrhea, decreased libido) - check prolactin/hormones if suspected
Hepatic function if symptoms suggest liver injury
counsel: Take this medicine only when you can stay in bed for a full night and right before bedtime
Do not take it with or after a heavy, fatty meal
Avoid alcohol and do not drive or operate machinery after taking it
Stop and seek urgent care if your face, tongue or throat swells or you have trouble breathing
Tell your doctor if your sleep does not improve, or if you notice mood changes, or any odd nighttime behaviors you do not remember
pk: Rapid - sleep onset typically aided within about 30 minutes
Ramelteon approximately 1-2.6 hours; active metabolite M-II approximately 2-5 hours
Short-acting; effects span the early sleep period
Store at 25 C (excursions 15-30 C permitted); protect from light
pearls: Ramelteon is NOT a controlled/scheduled substance - it has shown no evidence of abuse, dependence or withdrawal, distinguishing it from benzodiazepine and Z-drug hypnotics
Hepatic impairment, not renal, drives dose caution because of extensive first-pass metabolism via CYP1A2
Fluvoxamine is contraindicated due to a roughly 190-fold rise in exposure
A high-fat meal blunts and delays the effect - separate dosing from meals
Consider endocrine evaluation (prolactin, cortisol, testosterone) if a patient develops amenorrhea, galactorrhea, or decreased libido on therapy
missed: Ramelteon is taken only at bedtime when needed for sleep, so there is no make-up dose. If you forget to take it before bed, do not take it later in the night; simply resume the usual bedtime dose the following night.
overdose: There is limited experience with overdose. Expect exaggerated pharmacologic effects such as profound somnolence. Management is supportive with general symptomatic care, gastric lavage if appropriate, and monitoring; ensure airway protection. There is no specific antidote, and the value of dialysis is not established given high protein binding.
